clue.text: Partner in business suit

definitions.note: used as a verb, to partner someone at home

parts.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company, a business
a habit is a costume or outfit, as in a riding habit

explanation.surface: Someone in a firm wears a business suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partner' looks like a noun for someone in a firm, but here it is a verb: to live together as a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohabit is to live together as a couple without marrying, which is what domestic partners do.

clue.text: Chirpy bounder in the secret service

definitions.note: used as a noun, a chirping creature

indicators.note: in places the bounder inside the agency

parts.note: CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency
a bounder is a cad, an ill-mannered man

explanation.surface: A cheerful rogue works as a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chirpy' looks like a cheerful adjective, but it names an insect that chirps; 'bounder' also hints at its leaping.
explanation.definitionFit: This insect makes a loud chirping or buzzing song in summer.

clue.text: Not much of a sailor to lose a ship for

definitions.text: Not much of a sailor to lose a ship for

parts.words: Not much of a sailor to lose a ship for
parts.note: the old saying about spoiling a ship for a tiny amount of tar, a halfpenny's worth

explanation.surface: A poor seaman is not worth losing a vessel over.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'spoil the ship for a ha'porth of tar' means ruining something by stinting on a trifle; a halfpenny was the smallest British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A halfpenny's worth is a tiny amount, so this word means very little.

clue.text: Curator of a busy wax-works?

parts.note: a busy wax-works is a hive, where busy insects make wax, so its keeper is an apiarist

explanation.surface: Someone manages a crowded waxworks museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wax-works' looks like a waxworks museum such as Madame Tussauds, but bees make the wax.
explanation.definitionFit: An apiarist tends hives, where honeybees build wax combs.

clue.text: One well-equipped to blaze a trail?

definitions.text: One well-equipped to blaze a trail?

parts.words: One well-equipped to blaze a trail?
parts.note: to blaze a trail usually means to pioneer, but literally someone carrying a flame could set the path alight

explanation.surface: A pioneer has the right kit for the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blaze a trail' means to pioneer; read literally, it is setting fire along a path.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who carries a flame, literally or as a leader of a cause, is ready to light the way.

clue.text: Get on well with Mérimée

explanation.surface: Someone thrives in the company of a French novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Prosper Mérimée was the French author of the novella Carmen.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on well is to thrive or succeed; Mérimée's first name was Prosper.

clue.text: Normal knock-up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: a rap is a knock on a door

explanation.surface: A practice session is quite ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knock-up' looks like a tennis warm-up, but 'up' reverses RAP in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Par is the standard or average level, as in 'feeling below par'.

clue.text: Old university in France is very cut off and far out

indicators.note: cut off means the last letter of the French word is lopped

parts.note: tres is French for very

explanation.surface: An ancient French college is very remote and eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: TRES is French for 'very', and 'is' is a link word. 'Outré' keeps its French accent, which the grid ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré, borrowed from French, means unconventional or bizarre, which is what 'far out' means in slang.

clue.text: Sitting room for the maid?

parts.note: an old servant title names a housemaid after the front room where she waited on guests, so the room seems to be hers

explanation.surface: Is there somewhere for the servant to sit?
explanation.walkthrough: A parlourmaid was a housemaid who served at table and answered the door.
explanation.definitionFit: The parlour is an old-fashioned front room for receiving guests, a sitting room.

clue.text: Met head-on again, and forced back

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to butt is to strike with the head

explanation.surface: Two rams clashed once more and drove each other back.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebut an argument or attack is to repel it, to drive it back.

clue.text: Holder of the trophy is the one to provide the drinks

definitions.text: the one to provide the drinks

explanation.surface: The winner of the cup is expected to buy a round.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the first half is someone holding the cup they won; a court officer pouring wine had the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy is often a cup, so its holder bears it; historically a royal servant who served wine was given that title.

clue.text: Pulse beginning to beat after endless pain

indicators.note: after says the pain piece comes before the beat piece
endless means the final letter of the word for pain is dropped

parts.note: a throe is a spasm of pain

indicators.note: beginning to beat asks for the opening letter of that word

explanation.surface: A heartbeat starts up again once the pain has stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks like a verb or a lentil but is the definition; a throe is a pang.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a single strong beat, as of the pulse, so the two mean the same thing.

clue.text: It sounds as if the morning air is keen

definitions.text: It sounds as if the morning air is keen

parts.words: It sounds as if the morning air is keen
parts.note: the morning air said aloud is a mourning air, a sad tune, and keen here is the Irish word for a wail over the dead

explanation.surface: A fresh, sharp wind seems to blow at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' wants to mean sharp or cold, but here it means a lament; 'morning air' heard as 'mourning air' is a funeral song.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral song or lament, a keen, is a slow mournful tune sung for the dead.

clue.text: Laboriously contrive to get Beetle away

parts.note: a beetle is a heavy wooden mallet, a kind of hammer
out means away, as in 'out of the office'

explanation.surface: Someone struggles to get rid of an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beetle' has a capital to look like the insect, but it is the old word for a heavy mallet.
explanation.definitionFit: To work out a deal by long effort is to forge it, the way a smith shapes metal with blows.

clue.text: The thoughts of one in a main commuter station

indicators.note: in places the one inside the rearranged letters

parts.note: the main is the sea, and the Med is the Mediterranean

indicators.note: a commuter changes places daily, and to commute is to change, so the letters are switched around

parts.note: the Roman numeral one is I

explanation.surface: Someone muses while at a big railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commuter' rearranges the sea and STATION; Marcus Aurelius's Meditations is a famous book of thoughts.
explanation.definitionFit: Spells of deep contemplation produce reflections, and the plural word means thoughts set down.

clue.text: Weed in the old pastor's bag

parts.note: pastor is the Latin for shepherd, the old sense of the word
a purse is a small bag for money

explanation.surface: Something unwanted is found in an old clergyman's satchel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pastor' first meant a shepherd, from Latin; the weed's seed pods look like little pouches.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a common wild plant of the cabbage family, named for its pouch-shaped seed pods.

clue.text: Aristocratic name — superior girl!

parts.note: Patricia is a girl's name meaning noble, from Latin patricius

explanation.surface: A grand title belongs to a snooty young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Patricia comes from the Latin for a noble, so the girl is 'superior' by her name.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome the noble families formed one class, so the word describes the upper class.

clue.text: Expedition's communique

explanation.surface: A report from an exploring party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' means speed here, not a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition can mean promptness or speed, as in 'with all dispatch'; a dispatch is also an official message.

clue.text: Translate into a funny performance

parts.note: to interpret is to translate between languages

indicators.note: funny suggests the words into a are made odd, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone renders a text as a comic show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'performance' is the definition, as in an actor's reading of a role; 'funny' works only on INTO A.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's or musician's particular rendering of a role or piece is their reading of it, a performance.

clue.text: Curtail assembly concerned with peace

indicators.note: assembly suggests the letters of curtail are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: Cut down a meeting about a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembly' rearranges CURTAIL. The Trucial States, now the UAE, were named after truces with Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The word relates to a truce, a pause in fighting agreed between enemies.

clue.text: Won at Bisley, though bullet off the mark?

explanation.surface: Someone won a shooting match despite missing the target.
explanation.walkthrough: Bisley in Surrey is Britain's national shooting range; a bullet off the mark is shot out of line.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat someone at shooting is to outshoot them, and a shot that goes wide of its mark is an outshot one.

clue.text: Agree to despicable fellow being understudy

indicators.note: under places the fellow beneath the study piece in this down clue

parts.note: to con a text is to study it
a cur is a worthless man

explanation.surface: Someone accepts a lowly actor as a stand-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'understudy' looks like the theatre word, but it splits as 'under' and 'study' (CON).
explanation.definitionFit: To concur is to be of the same opinion, to agree.

clue.text: About £1 put by ham actor in "The Millionairess", for example

indicators.note: by places the second anagram beside the first
about signals that the letters of the first pieces are turned around and mixed

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

indicators.note: a ham performance is overdone, so the word actor is mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A small sum is put up by an overacting player in a Shaw comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' rearranges L and PUT into PLUT; 'ham' rearranges ACTOR into OCRAT. Shaw's play The Millionairess is about a very rich woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's title character is a very rich woman, and a person whose wealth gives them power is a plutocrat.

clue.text: Animal is all right up-state, I concluded

parts.note: OK means all right

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the state's letters read upwards

parts.note: PA is Pennsylvania, a US state

explanation.surface: An animal is fine in the north of the state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up-state' looks like a region, but 'up' reverses PA; I comes last, as 'concluded' suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: The okapi is an African animal related to the giraffe.

clue.text: Short presentation to someone in buckskin trousers

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words buckskin trousers

explanation.surface: A brief introduction is made to a frontiersman in leather breeches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to someone' is padding that keeps the picture of meeting a frontiersman; the answer straddles 'buckskin' and 'trousers'.
explanation.definitionFit: A clipped form of introduction, the brief opening of a talk or piece of music.

clue.text: Army sends back a soldier to the subarctic forests

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

indicators.note: sends back means the words a soldier are read from the end

parts.note: GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: The army returns a soldier to the far northern woods.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is Britain's Territorial Army; only 'a soldier' turns, not the Army.
explanation.definitionFit: The belt of coniferous woodland across Siberia and Canada, just south of the tundra, goes by this Russian name.

clue.text: Of the later Stone Age, with a kind of lichen round it

indicators.note: a kind of suggests a variant form of lichen, so its letters with the others are reordered

parts.note: a round shape looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Something prehistoric is covered in a sort of lichen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a kind of' rearranges LICHEN with O and IT into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Stone Age, when farming began, is the later part of the Stone Age.

clue.text: Note: the infinite ordinal number is not specified

indicators.note: infinite means the word the loses its end letter

explanation.surface: A remark on numbers without limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'infinite' (without end) drops the E from THE.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'to the nth degree' uses an unspecified ordinal, meaning an indefinitely large position in a series.

clue.text: Infernal sex psychologist besieged by husbands

indicators.note: besieged by says the psychologist is surrounded by the two husbands

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband, so two husbands give two Hs
Havelock Ellis was a pioneering British writer on human sexuality

explanation.surface: A dreadful sexologist is mobbed by angry husbands.
explanation.walkthrough: Havelock Ellis (1859-1939) was the British doctor who wrote Studies in the Psychology of Sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Infernal means of the underworld or fiendish, the same as belonging to the place of damnation.

clue.text: Surely not one to conceal treason?

definitions.text: Surely not one to conceal treason?

indicators.note: concealing the word treason means disguising it by moving its letters around

explanation.surface: A statesman would never cover up treachery, surely?
explanation.walkthrough: 'to conceal' disguises TREASON by rearranging it; read whole, the clue asks whether a lawmaker would hide treachery.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a legislative upper house, such as Rome's or the US's, ought to be loyal to the state.
